To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the radiation dose required for data collection can be estimated from the initial diffraction data, (2) the dose can be estimated from a single diffraction image and (3) the dose can also be estimated from the statistics of the data set.
the data statistics of a diffraction experiment can be modelled in terms of the crystal quality, the radiation dose, beam aperture, oscillation width and resolution limit.
the radiation-dose requirement for a given crystal is determined primarily by the crystal size, and secondarily by the crystal quality and the resolution limit.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new strategies for the collection of high-quality data from macromolecular crystals.
the quantitative analysis of the X-ray data-collection strategy.
the quantitative description of the data-collection process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best way to obtain a data set of the highest quality is to collect the data in a series of short exposures, with the shortest possible oscillation widths.
the data-collection strategy is not as simple and straightforward as is often thought.
, for the best possible diffraction data, the beam aperture and the oscillation angle are not independent parameters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the radiation-dose requirement for a data set of a given resolution is a function of the crystal quality and that it can be reduced by increasing the redundancy of the data.
the data statistics can be modelled and predicted from the diffraction images and that the model is useful in the design of data-collection strategies.
the radiation damage is not the major factor limiting the resolution of the data set, but rather the radiation-damage-induced reduction in crystal quality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the best strategy for data collection is not necessarily the one that gives the best resolution limit, but rather the one that gives a data set with the best statistics for refinement.
the best strategy to collect data is to collect as many images as possible with the smallest oscillations, the largest crystal-to-detector distances and the smallest detector pixel size.
the data quality is determined by the crystal quality and the radiation dose, rather than by the crystal size.
